# Strictly compatible smooth local minima: an exact finite-mass exclusion

## Theorem and scope

Let P be a finite lattice-convex base set and let K_p be positive
d-dimensional actual fibers, with d>=2. Assume:

* the family has the strict compatibility margin defined in
  `candidate 97eab0f821e54041`;
* every K_p has C1 strictly convex boundary;
* the family is an unrestricted local minimum of its maximum normalized
  ambient closed-halfspace depth beta among actual positive families on P.

Then

    beta>=1/(2h(P)),                                    (1)

where h(P) is the finite Helly number of P for convex-set traces. Therefore
such a local minimum cannot violate the stronger finite-base target
Gamma_d/h(P), since Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d<=1/2.

The compression and its conditional radial conclusion already appear in
`candidate 1140440dbc94280d`. The additional result here
is a full geometric realization of its independent signed directions
under the stated strict compatibility and own-fiber regularity: finitely
many exposed hull additions and trims with exact prescribed masses suffice.
An ambient uniformly convex defining function, differentiability of the
maximizing center, and a smooth radial boundary velocity are unnecessary.

This does not extend to active compatibility or flat fibers. The smooth
ball-cylinder example in the two-sided note gives a rigorous obstruction
to dropping the first hypothesis. Nor does an approximation by this open
phase preserve the property of being a local minimum.

## 1. Compress whole circuit groups, keeping their projected coverage

Write M for the mixed mass and Q=beta M. At every fiber's restricted
maximum choose one positive critical continuous-normal circuit, as in the
exact critical-cap archive. Positive depth forces its center into the
interior of the positive fiber. For group i, anchored at p_i, write

    H_ij={ (p,x): a_ij.p+u_ij.x>=b_ij }, |u_ij|=1,
    sum_j rho_ij u_ij=0, rho_ij>0,
    A_i=sum_j rho_ij a_ij,
    h_i=sum_j rho_ij b_ij=A_i.p_i.

Every cap in group i has its own restricted maximum raw mass Q_i<=Q.
The projected closed halfspace G_i={p:A_i.p>=h_i} contains p_i. Wherever
G_i holds, the group's weighted margins sum to a nonnegative number
independently of x, so its closed caps cover the ENTIRE continuous plane.
Thus the G_i cover P. This includes A_i=0, in which case h_i=0 and the
group covers every base.

By definition, h(P) is the least integer h such that every finite family
of convex sets whose intersection misses P has a subfamily of at most h
with the same property. It is finite, since h(P)<=|P|. Replace each open
complement of G_i by a closed halfspace with the same trace on finite P;
if its trace is empty use the empty convex set. A sufficiently small
parallel shift realizes every nonempty trace because P is finite.
The complements have empty intersection on P. Applying h(P) and taking
complements selects at most h(P) WHOLE circuit groups covering P.

A selected group of raw mass Q_i<Q cannot cover any deepest base: its
caps would cover that fiber's deepest candidate with mass below Q.
Therefore the selected deepest-origin groups cover all deepest bases.
Let their number be k, with 1<=k<=h(P). Add back each nondeep base's
original group as a slack cover. These added groups have Q_i<Q and need
no count in the first-order comparison.

The selected deepest-origin groups have distinct anchors, because only
one original group was chosen per base. We keep the integer normals,
continuous normals, and circuit weights fixed. Threshold perturbations
with sum_j rho_ij delta b_ij=0 keep h_i, and therefore G_i, EXACTLY fixed.
Consequently these compressed groups continue to cover every assigned
fiber plane under the deformations below, not merely their anchors.

## 2. Two exposed boundary points realize a central half-mass direction

Fix one selected anchor p_i and its interior maximizing center x_i. For
each direction v on the unit sphere, let w_i^+(v) and w_i^-(v) be the two
points where the rays x_i+t v and x_i-t v meet boundary K_p_i. Radial
projection about an interior point is a homeomorphism between the sphere
and a convex body's boundary.

Choose v such that neither boundary point lies on any cap plane from the
finite selected list. Such a choice exists for d>=2. The intersection of
any affine hyperplane with a C1 strictly convex boundary has empty
relative interior: a boundary patch contained in a hyperplane would
contain a line segment by its local C1 graph, contradicting strict
convexity. Its preimage under radial projection is closed with empty
interior. The same is true after the antipodal map v->-v. A finite union
of these closed sets cannot cover the sphere, since their complements
are open dense. This also proves the assertion in d=2.

Every own cap in group i passes through x_i. The two ray endpoints lie
strictly on opposite sides of its plane, so

    [1_H_ij(w_i^+)+1_H_ij(w_i^-)]/2=1/2.                (2)

Strict compatibility makes every singleton own support point globally
exposed, by Section 1 of
`candidate 571b5ceb2d4e114a`. C1 strict
convexity provides the unique normal and singleton support face. Thus
both points satisfy ALL hypotheses of the signed local-mass theorem.

For a real parameter eta_i, prescribe signed mass epsilon eta_i/2 at
each of w_i^+ and w_i^-. Positive masses are exact local convex-hull bumps;
negative masses are exact exposed trims. Doing this simultaneously for
all k anchors is feasible, with total mass

    M_epsilon=M+epsilon sum_i eta_i.                    (3)

The changed regions are disjoint and approach the selected points. The
chosen cap-boundary gaps make their incidence identities exact, even
after cap thresholds move by O(epsilon). This construction uses no
unproved compatibility repair step.

## 3. Finite comparison roots and their probability balance

All selected cap threshold slopes are positive and have equal traces.
Indeed each own anchor has a proper interior section of positive area.
In every other strictly convex fiber a supporting section is at most a
point and has zero (d-1)-volume for d>=2; proper sections have continuous
area. Thus no coincident supporting-facet slope remains.

Let S_ij be that common slope and put

    kappa_ij=(rho_ij/S_ij)/sum_l(rho_il/S_il),
    B_iq=sum_j kappa_ij
       [1_H_ij(w_q^+)+1_H_ij(w_q^-)]/2.

Then

    0<=B_iq<=1,       B_ii=1/2.                         (4)

For the arbitrary vector eta, the body-mass change of cap H_ij, divided
by epsilon, is

    g_ij=sum_q eta_q
          [1_H_ij(w_q^+)+1_H_ij(w_q^-)]/2.

Put a_i=sum_j kappa_ij g_ij=sum_q B_iq eta_q and move its threshold by
epsilon(g_ij-a_i)/S_ij. The rho-weighted sum is exactly zero, so the
ENTIRE projected covering halfspace G_i is retained. The actual mass of
each adjusted cap is Q+epsilon a_i+o(epsilon). The nondeep groups keep
their strict slack, since total changed mass is O(epsilon). Hence the
whole source, including all moved candidates, is covered by these caps,
and

    limsup_(epsilon down to0)(D_epsilon-beta)/epsilon
       <=(1/M) max_i sum_q(B_iq-beta)eta_q.               (5)

At a local minimum the maximum on the right cannot be negative for any
real eta. Strict separation of the finite convex hull of its row vectors
from zero would give such an eta. Consequently there is a probability
vector pi on the k selected groups satisfying

    sum_i pi_i B_iq=beta for each q.                     (6)

Using nonnegativity and the diagonal entry in (4), equation (6) implies

    beta>=pi_q/2.

Summing over q yields k beta>=1/2. Since k<=h(P), this proves (1).

Finally, (1+1/d)^d>=2 by its first two binomial terms, so Gamma_d<=1/2.
For lattice-convex P one also has the standard Doignon bound h(P)<=2^n,
but no such bound is needed for the stated finite-base conclusion.

The argument is an exclusion of bad LOCAL MINIMA within the explicit
strictly compatible smooth phase. It does not assert that every family
in this phase itself has depth at least 1/(2h(P)), and it does not move an
arbitrary attained minimizer into this phase. Those distinctions prevent
using the conditional theorem as a proof of (OC).
